--- the link card on @yetanotheruseless.com's quoted post: https://atilloy.com/2026/11/16/the-short-age-of-dragon-riders/
(the page's text)
The short age of dragon riders | Antoine Tilloy’s research log Context
Since approximately August of this year, the AI models available to the public have passed a threshold: in a proper harness, they are stronger than most theoretical physicists (myself included) at most technical tasks. What counts as “technical” exactly is blurry (and likely to expand) but I take it to include the bulk of what junior theoretical physicists were doing day to day during their PhDs.
Concretely, the models are now able to carry out complex analytical calculations, work out lengthy proofs, turn well-posed problems into code, all with minimal input. They iterate, correct their errors, launch simulations to verify their conjectures, and summarize their work. On my own problems, I have already seen the impossible being done several times, starting with Fable 5 in May (I reported some on X and LinkedIn ). Those who deny this progress have just not tried hard enough (with the latest models), or are blinded by their ego.
As of November 2026, the best public models still lack research taste. They execute beautifully when given a clear goal but are worse than the best researchers at coming up with good questions, or at having the sparks of creativity needed to get out of a dead end. They do not have as much vision as the best humans.
This situation is unlikely to persist. Even if the whole internet has been exhausted to pre-train models, the availability of human data is no longer the bottleneck. Thanks to reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), models can improve simply by solving new tasks, and are in no way bound by human intelligence.
At least in the immediate future, progress is thus predictable. First, the internal models at OpenAI and Anthropic have now solved countless open problems, showing that they are indeed a generation ahead of what the public currently has access to (which is already superhuman at many tasks). Second, computing power, the only bottleneck, has been increasing steadily, far beyond what was used to train the current best models. Unless the scaling laws surprisingly break down, we have two generations of improvements ahead of us without doing anything new. On top of this, recursive self-improvement is under way, at least in the weak sense that strong models already substantially help design the training environments of their successors. In a nutshell, as long as the datacenters survive kinetic strikes or a grassroots Butlerian Jihad, progress is not going to stop.
Like most scientists, I am conflicted. All the friction is gone; problems melt before we can even understand the solution. It is great, and also scary, leading some in the community to hate the models. I have always been a techno-optimist absolutist. It would be a betrayal to flip now that the wave of progress touches my craft. No, even if it burns me, I still think we should steal the fire!
Granted, the fire, this time, may come with existential risks for humanity. I think these risks are real, and to leading order, better understood by the nerds in Silicon Valley than by skeptics like Yann LeCun. Alignment research is certainly important, and if slowing down training helps reduce existential risk, then we probably should.
But I think it is too easy to reject AI progress for wrong, self-serving reasons, under the guise of a legitimate concern for mankind. And thus, while one should take these risks seriously, it is important to also think about what is left for us in case they are solved.
It is still too difficult for me to envision what the steady state may look like, or whether there will even be one. But I would like to discuss what I think we should do (or at least what I am doing) during the transient period of symbiotic human-AI discovery.
Grief
The first step is to quickly go through the five stages of grief. Mathematicians, as Sylvia Serfaty recently noted in her talk at the IHP , at least seem to have gone through the denial phase. Physicists are likely only three months behind.
Prominent mathematicians, even those who were dismissing AI only three months ago, are no longer denying its power. However, the most visible public reaction, initiated by 25 Fields medalists , is terrible in a way that can only be explained by shock. The best problem solvers alive are now claiming that results, proofs, technical breakthroughs, which in many cases gave them their status and fame, were not really the goal. The goal was the friends we made along the way: the serendipitous discoveries, the mathematical community that got built, the long hours spent pondering in front of a blackboard. This enjoyment, this human understanding, for the community and by the community, is what had value all along.
I disagree. I think we deserve all the bad things that will happen to us if we react like such sore losers. Serendipitous discoveries are important, but first, it is unclear that AIs will necessarily lead to fewer, and second, the end results clearly mattered and still matter. Seeing the process as an end in itself, rather than a means to an end, is profoundly self-serving, and sadly typical of academia.
We have to accept that many things we were doing, sometimes with joy, are already gone. I have spent days massaging an equation to bring it into a form that worked, proud of my virtuosity. I have made complicated calculations with pen and paper, covering entire notebooks to get an answer I could trust. I have spent weeks turning computations into code, and optimized the implementation over months, to be the first to extract certain results from theory. I have fine-tuned plots for hours until they looked pretty. Science was slow; all these steps were important and had to be taught. They were sometimes tedious, sometimes meditative, and tied to our identity. I was good at this, and enjoyed at least a fraction of it. But even if the models do not make any progress, which as I argued is highly unlikely, this is gone .
